questions.problem:
Given the matrices

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\,B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}]\,v=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

 in which of the following expressions is the Hadamard product well-defined?

I. ${B}^{T}A⊙B\,\text{diag}(v)$

II. $A⊙B{v}^{T}$

III. $AB⊙B{v}^{T}v$

*Hint: Here, $\text{diag}(v)$ is a diagonal matrix with the entries of $v$ on the diagonal.*
questions.worked_solution:
The Hadamard product of two matrices (or vectors) is only defined if they have the same dimensions.

First, notice that $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix, $B$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix, and $v$ is a $1\times 3$ row vector.

Now, let's consider each expression in turn:

- The dimensions of ${B}^{T}A$ are $3\times 2,$ and the dimensions of $B\,\text{diag}(v)$ are $2\times 3.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression I is *not* well-defined.

- The dimensions of $A$ are $2\times 2,$ and the dimensions of $B{v}^{T}$ are $2\times 1.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression II is *not* well-defined.

- The dimensions of $AB$ are $2\times 3,$ and the dimensions of $B{v}^{T}v$ are $2\times 3.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression III is well-defined.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

questions.worked_solution:
For compatible matrices $A,$ $B,$ and $C,$ and scalar $\alpha ,$ the Hadamard product has the following properties:

- Commutativity:

$$
A⊙B=B⊙A
$$

- Associativity:

$$
(A⊙B)⊙C=A⊙(B⊙C)
$$

- Distributivity over Addition:

$$
A⊙(B+C)=A⊙B+A⊙C
$$

- Scalar Distributivity:

$$
\alpha (A⊙B)=(\alpha A)⊙B=A⊙(\alpha B)
$$

In this case, by the scalar distributivity of the Hadamard product, we have

$$
(\alpha Y)⊙X+{Z}^{T}=\alpha (Y⊙X)+{Z}^{T}.
$$

Then, by the commutativity of the Hadamard product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (Y⊙X)+{Z}^{T} & =\alpha (X⊙Y)+{Z}^{T} \\  & =3[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}]+{[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}]}^{T} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -3 \\ -9 & 12\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-5 & 4 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6-5 & -3+4 \\ -9+2 & 12-3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -7 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$ A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2\end{aligned}],\,y=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]. $$ Given the matrices above, write $A{x}^{T}⊙(y+{x}^{T})$ as a matrix product.
$A{x}^{T}⊙(y+{x}^{T})=\,\,$ {{field-1}} $0$ $-5$
$0$ {{field-2}} {{field-3}}
questions.worked_solution:
The Hadamard product of two compatible vectors $u$ and $v$ can be expressed as the matrix product

$$
v⊙u=\text{diag}(v)u.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A{x}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8\end{aligned}]
$$

and

$$
y+{x}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that they are of the same size; hence, their Hadamard product is well-defined. We conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}A{x}^{T}⊙(y+{x}^{T}) & =\text{diag}(A{x}^{T})(y+{x}^{T}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
